differences.title: 1. INDEXING ENGINE
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant primarily uses HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) for ANN, maintaining layered graphs per collection. It supports quantization and payload-aware filtering, optimizing traversal and distance computations at query time.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate supports configurable vector index types via modules and schema-driven configuration. Under the hood, it builds ANN indexes (often HNSW) and can route queries through module pipelines for vectorization and reranking.

differences.title: 2. SCHEMA & DATA MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant uses explicit collections with vector configuration (size, distance metric), and stores payload fields alongside vectors. Filtering works directly on payload metadata with fast bitmap/segment intersections during candidate selection.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate uses a schema with “classes” and typed properties. Modules can manage vectorization at ingest time, while GraphQL/REST queries combine semantic vectors with property filters defined by the schema.

differences.title: 3. HYBRID SEARCH PIPELINE
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant hybrid behavior is typically achieved by combining vector similarity with structured payload filters. It can also store multiple vectors and use weighted scoring strategies to approximate blended relevance.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate’s hybrid search commonly uses BM25-style keyword scoring alongside vector similarity, then blends scores (e.g., alpha weighting). The combination is performed in the query pipeline to improve recall for lexical matches.

differences.title: 4. MULTI-TENANCY & ISOLATION
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant provides strong collection-level isolation patterns and supports sharding via its distributed architecture. With payload-driven filtering and separate collections, you can isolate tenants while keeping per-collection index locality.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate offers multi-tenancy features that isolate data and vectors by tenant within the same instance. Query routing respects tenant scoping, while index structures remain organized to limit cross-tenant leakage.

differences.title: 5. UPDATE / UPSERT BEHAVIOR
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant stores vectors and payload in segments and can update points via upsert, then compacts/optimizes segments asynchronously. Index maintenance keeps HNSW graphs consistent without rebuilding the entire collection each write.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate supports adding/updating objects that affects both vector entries and schema properties. Index updates are handled by the underlying ANN structures and module pipelines, often with asynchronous consistency depending on configuration.

differences.title: 6. SCALING & DISTRIBUTION
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant uses a sharded architecture with replicas, distributing collections across nodes for horizontal scaling. Query fan-out occurs across shards, merging top-k results while applying payload filters consistently per shard.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate clusters similarly shard data but organize routing around class/tenant structures. Requests are distributed across nodes, and results are merged centrally, with replication used for fault tolerance and read throughput.

differences.title: 7. OPERATOR EXPERIENCE & ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: Qdrant tends to be simpler to operate for vector-only workloads: fewer moving parts beyond storage, indexing, and optional quantization. You can bring your own embeddings, keeping the runtime surface small.
differences.rightDesc: Weaviate’s module ecosystem (e.g., vectorizers, rerankers) can integrate embedding generation and post-retrieval steps inside the database layer. This accelerates time-to-demo but increases configuration and dependency management.
